extracted.intended_audience: researchers in science communication, scientometrics, and institutional press officers
extracted.subtask_description: Quantitative and textual analysis of research-based press releases on EurekAlert!, focusing on classification of research (basic vs applied), text similarity and readability, topical and institutional distributions, and temporal trends (2015–2022).

rubrics_metrics.name: EurekAlert! eligibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases published on EurekAlert! must meet specific eligibility criteria, including the requirement that they be posted by public information officers (PIOs) employed at eligible organisations that conduct, publish, or fund scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only submissions satisfying the platform's eligibility are accepted; organisations (universities, publishers, government agencies, corporations, etc.) pay a fee to submit. Journalists may apply for reporter access to view embargoed releases and supporting publicity materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aims and role of academic press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic press releases are typically based on presenting the results of individual research papers, aiming to explain new findings in accessible language, provide context and highlight their scientific novelty or societal relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases serve a dual strategic and communicative role: to attract media uptake and to communicate directly with the public; usually written/distributed by marketing and PR staff and act as science communication objects (SCOs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria used by institutional press officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Press officers decide which research articles to promote and are expected to select research that aligns with contemporary journalistic news values, particularly work addressing issues relevant to everyday life (e.g., health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the primary aim is to attract media attention, research with greater perceived newsworthiness (often applied, societally relevant work) is likelier to be selected; this is an explicit hypothesis and observed tendency discussed in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and jargon removal for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A key task for press officers is the translation of scientific content to make it accessible, which includes removing the jargon that often characterises academic papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing jargon improves processing fluency and audience engagement; practitioners must balance simplification with factual accuracy. References cite evidence that jargon hinders comprehension and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing scientific accuracy with media appeal (news values)
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing press releases, press officers must adhere to scientific norms of accuracy and objectivity while enhancing media appeal by responding to news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This boundary-spanning role requires specialised media knowledge and careful negotiation between integrity and newsworthiness; anti-patterns include compromising accuracy for promotional spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release linkage requirement to research paper (DOI mention)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the study dataset, only press releases that mentioned a scientific article via a DOI were retained for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioning a DOI enables matching press releases to the corresponding research paper metadata (titles, abstracts, journal, affiliations) in databases like OpenAlex; press releases without DOIs are excluded from DOI-based analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset inclusion & matching procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Dataset construction filtered EurekAlert! press releases (collected via web-crawling) to the 2015–2022 period, kept releases that mentioned a DOI, and matched those DOIs to research papers in OpenAlex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial crawl identified ~495,180 releases; filtering for DOI mentions produced 129,319 releases, with 116,777 finally matched to OpenAlex. These procedural filters determine which press releases are analyzable in DOI-linked scientometric work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification into broad research fields (OpenAlex / Van Eck & Waltman approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign papers (and their linked press releases) to five broad main fields using a publication-level classification that algorithmically clusters articles into many research areas based on citation relationships (predecessor of Van Eck & Waltman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The approach links clustered areas to five broad fields; the same field assigned to the press release for cross-field comparisons. Use of this algorithmic classification is a standard for field-level analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification into research levels (basic vs applied) using Boyack et al. 2014
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Boyack et al.'s multinomial logistic regression classification (originally four levels: basic scientific research, applied research, engineering-technological mix, applied technology) trained on titles/abstracts/references to assign research level, then re-label into two levels: basic research and applied research (all non-basic relabeled as applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The original four-level model is combined into two to increase balance and interpretability. The method relies on textual and citation features and the trained model distributed by Boyack et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text similarity measurement (TF-IDF vector space & cosine similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure textual similarity between press releases and corresponding research papers using a TF-IDF-weight vector space model to construct vectors (titles and full texts) and cosine similarity to quantify overlap (especially used on titles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TF-IDF evaluates term importance via term frequency and inverse document frequency; cosine similarity measures angle between vectors. Note limitation: TF-IDF similarity captures word overlap rather than semantic equivalence. Typical observed title similarity range ~0.2–0.4 (modest overlap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability measurement (Flesch Reading Ease Score, FRES)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess readability of press releases (full texts) and research-paper abstracts using the Flesch Reading Ease Score (RE), computed from words per sentence and syllables per word, where higher RE indicates easier text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula: RE = 206.835 − 1.105(total words/total sentences) − 84.6(total syllables/total words). Interpretive ranges: 90–100 very easy, 50–60 high-school level, 30–50 college level, 0–30 very complex. Caveat: FRES has been criticised for focusing on superficial linguistic features but is widely used for longer texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyword co-occurrence mapping for topical basic/applied orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use EurekAlert!'s assigned keywords to build co-occurrence maps; colour or other summarisation indicates the average basic (coded 1) vs applied (coded 2) nature of research papers linked to those keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps can be produced overall and per broad field to visualise which topics are associated with basic vs applied research; interactive maps can provide drill-down and co-occurrence structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distribution analysis of press releases (2015–2022)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse counts and shares of press releases related to basic vs applied research over time to detect trends, growth rates, and anomalies (e.g., COVID-19-related shifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare absolute numbers and proportions; observe differential growth rates (paper finds basic-research releases increased faster overall but share declined 2021–2022, possibly due to COVID-19 focus on applied research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional origin metrics (journals, author affiliations, issuing institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate which journals, author affiliations, and institutions issue or are featured in press releases, and split these counts by basic vs applied research orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce top-N lists and breakdowns (e.g., top 15 journals/institutions), interpret institutional mission/context (e.g., hospitals emphasizing applied research), and consider publisher/journal promotion practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of title adaptation as proxy for press-officer translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the similarity between press-release titles and research-article titles (TF-IDF cosine) as a proxy for the extent to which press officers adapt or 'translate' research titles for accessibility and media appeal; lower similarity indicates greater adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: applied-research article titles are more similar to press-release titles than basic-research titles; no category exceeded similarity >0.4, showing frequent retitling. Interpret cautiously because TF-IDF measures lexical overlap, not meaning-preserving paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability gap comparison (press releases vs abstracts) as accessibility indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare FRES scores of press releases (full text) and paper abstracts to assess how much press releases increase accessibility relative to the scholarly abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases generally score higher (easier) than abstracts across fields; applied-research abstracts often more readable than basic-research abstracts, but press-release adaptation reduces the readability gap between basic and applied.
